title: Use Call and Respond to Check Calculator Use
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton applies his favourite participation technique, Call and Respond, to a specific and often-overlooked problem: students who understand the maths but don't know the order of buttons to press on a calculator. He admits to previously either missing this issue or assuming that simply explaining the button order once would be enough for students to remember it. His alternative is a scripted Call and Respond routine, demonstrated in full for a trigonometry calculation, where the teacher models each step (SHIFT, then SIN, then bracket-number-bracket, then equals) while students chorus back the key word for each step, building in repetition and emphasis on tricky vocabulary like 'trigonometric.' The routine ends with students immediately talking a partner through the same steps on their own calculator, converting the choral rehearsal into individual practice.
points: Barton frames calculator button order as an overlooked 'Achilles heel' that can undermine students who otherwise understand the underlying maths.
He uses Call and Respond to make button-order instructions stick, having students chorus back each step (SHIFT, SIN, brackets, equals) rather than just listening to a one-time explanation.
The script deliberately repeats and re-emphasizes tricky vocabulary — pausing to have students chorus 'trigonometric ratio we need' twice and correcting pronunciation mid-routine.
The routine closes by immediately handing the explanation over to students, who talk a partner through the same calculator steps to convert the choral response into individual retrieval.
quotes: An Achilles heel for many maths students is their calculator use. They could be the world’s leading experts at trigonometry, negative numbers or the quadratic formula, but if they don’t know the order in which to press the buttons on their calculators, then they are likely to come unstuck.
In the past, I have either been ignorant of this issue (due to the curse of knowledge ), or assumed that by explaining the order to students they would listen and remember.

Better teachers than me will carefully model the order the buttons need to be pressed and get the students to practice at the same time. But I think the effectiveness of all scenarios can be aided by a lovely bit of Call and Respond.
Teacher: Okay, so watch me. First, we press SHIFT because we want to find the size of an angle. What do we press first?…
Teacher: Once more, be careful how we say trig-on-o-met-ric. Next, we press SIN because it is the…
Okay, in a moment, not now, you are going to show your partner how to do this on your calculator and talk them through the steps. The person closest to the door goes first… Ready?… Wait for it… Go!
